walkthroughs.body_html:
Strong: HCl, H2SO4, HNO3 - fully ionised.

Weak: ethanoic acid - partly ionised.

Strength!= concentration.

Acid + alkali: H+ + OH- -> H2O.

Precipitation: Ag+ + Cl- -> AgCl.

2HCl + CaCO3 -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

Effervescence is observed.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
options: Strong and concentrated mean the same thing for acids.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
A strong acid fully dissociates in water; a concentrated acid has a high amount of acid per volume — these are independent properties.

mcqs.q: What happens to electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine?
options: Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Sodium and chlorine share an electron between them.
Sodium loses one electron to chlorine; the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions attract electrostatically.

mcqs.q: When an acid neutralises an alkali, what is the pH of the resulting solution?
options: Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH exactly 7 regardless of the acid and base used.
Approximately 7 if equivalent amounts of strong acid and strong alkali react — but it varies with strength.
